chapter_text:
CHAPTER 8 - ABSORPTION, TRANSPORT AND WATER LOSS IN PLANTS

Introduction

A large tree may absorb hundreds of litres of water from the soil in a single day, lift much of it to leaves tens of metres above the ground, and lose most of it to the air as vapour - all without a heart or muscles to pump it. How is this possible? This chapter explains the physical principles of water movement (diffusion, imbibition and osmosis), the water relations of a plant cell (water potential, turgor and plasmolysis), how roots absorb water and minerals, how sap rises to the top of tall trees, the loss of water by transpiration and its control by stomata, and finally how food made in the leaves is transported through the phloem to the rest of the plant.

8.1 WATER RELATIONS OF PLANT CELLS

DIFFUSION is the net movement of molecules or ions from a region of their HIGHER concentration to a region of their LOWER concentration, that is, DOWN a concentration gradient. It is a passive process needing no energy from the cell. Diffusion is important in gaseous exchange (entry of carbon dioxide and exit of oxygen and water vapour through stomata) and in the movement of ions.

IMBIBITION is a special type of diffusion in which water is absorbed by solid hydrophilic (water-loving) colloidal substances, causing them to swell. Dry seeds swell when soaked because their cellulose, starch and proteins imbibe water. The enormous pressure developed during imbibition (imbibition pressure) can split rocks and was used in old times to break stones; it is also the force that helps a germinating seedling push through the soil.

OSMOSIS is the movement of solvent (water) molecules from a region of higher water concentration (dilute or weak solution) to a region of lower water concentration (concentrated or strong solution) THROUGH a SELECTIVELY PERMEABLE (semipermeable) membrane. The membrane allows water to pass but not the dissolved solutes. When a plant cell is placed in a solution, water moves in or out by osmosis:
 - ENDOSMOSIS is the movement of water INTO the cell when it is placed in a hypotonic (weaker) solution such as pure water; the cell swells and becomes turgid.
 - EXOSMOSIS is the movement of water OUT OF the cell when it is placed in a hypertonic (stronger) solution; the cell loses water and shrinks.

OSMOTIC PRESSURE (OP) is the pressure that must be applied to a solution to just prevent the entry of water into it through a semipermeable membrane. A concentrated solution has a HIGH osmotic pressure; pure water has zero osmotic pressure. Osmotic pressure increases with the concentration of solute.

When water enters a plant cell by endosmosis, the protoplasm swells and pushes against the cell wall. The pressure exerted by the swollen cell contents against the wall is the TURGOR PRESSURE, and a cell that is firm and distended in this way is said to be TURGID. The rigid cellulose cell wall pushes back with an equal and opposite WALL PRESSURE. Turgidity keeps non-woody (herbaceous) parts of the plant firm and erect; loss of turgor causes wilting.

WATER POTENTIAL (symbol psi, the Greek letter psi) is the modern way of describing the water status of a cell. It is the tendency of water to move from one place to another. By convention, the water potential of PURE water at standard temperature and pressure is taken as ZERO. Adding solute to water LOWERS its water potential, making it NEGATIVE. Water always moves from a region of HIGHER (less negative) water potential to a region of LOWER (more negative) water potential. Water potential has two main components:
 - SOLUTE POTENTIAL (osmotic potential, psi_s): the reduction in water potential due to dissolved solutes. It is always NEGATIVE; the more concentrated the solution, the more negative psi_s.
 - PRESSURE POTENTIAL (psi_p): the effect of pressure on water potential. In a turgid cell the wall pressure makes psi_p POSITIVE.
These combine as psi = psi_s + psi_p (water potential = solute potential + pressure potential). Water potential decides the direction of water movement between cells and between the soil and the root.

PLASMOLYSIS is the shrinkage of the protoplasm (living contents) of a plant cell away from its cell wall when the cell is placed in a strongly hypertonic solution. Water leaves the cell by exosmosis, the protoplasm contracts, and the cell membrane pulls away from the wall. Such a cell is said to be PLASMOLYSED and its turgor pressure falls to zero. If a plasmolysed cell is transferred back to pure water in time, water re-enters and the protoplasm swells again to press against the wall - this recovery is called DEPLASMOLYSIS. Plasmolysis proves that the cell membrane is selectively permeable and that the cell is alive; a dead cell cannot be plasmolysed. Excessive salting of soil or fertiliser can plasmolyse and kill root cells.

8.2 ABSORPTION OF WATER BY ROOTS

Water and dissolved minerals are absorbed mainly through the ROOT HAIRS - fine, thin-walled, tubular outgrowths of the epidermal (piliferous layer) cells near the root tips. Root hairs greatly INCREASE the surface area for absorption and are in close contact with the film of water around soil particles. The cell sap inside a root hair is more concentrated (has a lower, more negative water potential) than the dilute soil solution, so water enters the root hair by osmosis, then passes from cell to cell across the cortex towards the xylem.

Water crosses the root by two PATHWAYS:
 - the APOPLAST pathway: water travels through the non-living parts of the cells - the cell walls and the intercellular spaces - without crossing any membrane. This is a fast route. At the endodermis the waterproof band of suberin called the CASPARIAN STRIP blocks the apoplast and forces water into the symplast.
 - the SYMPLAST pathway: water moves through the living contents (cytoplasm) of the cells, passing from one cell to the next through fine cytoplasmic bridges called PLASMODESMATA.

Absorption is of two kinds. PASSIVE ABSORPTION accounts for most of the water uptake in a rapidly transpiring plant: transpiration from the leaves creates a pull (tension) that is transmitted down to the roots, and the roots act merely as passive surfaces through which water is drawn in; no metabolic energy of the root is used. ACTIVE ABSORPTION occurs slowly and uses the metabolic energy (respiration, ATP) of the root cells to take in water, often against or independent of transpiration; it is linked with the active uptake of ions and is responsible for root pressure. Active absorption is significant when transpiration is low, for example at night or in the early morning.

8.3 ASCENT OF SAP

The upward movement of water and dissolved minerals from the roots to the leaves through the XYLEM is called the ASCENT OF SAP. In tall trees this water column may have to be raised more than a hundred metres. The xylem vessels and tracheids form continuous, non-living, tube-like channels ideally suited for this bulk flow. Two mechanisms contribute:

ROOT PRESSURE is a positive hydrostatic pressure that develops in the xylem of the roots as a result of the active absorption of water and ions by living root cells. It can push water a little way up the stem and is shown by GUTTATION and by the bleeding of sap from a cut stump. However, root pressure is small (rarely more than 1-2 atmospheres), is absent in many trees and in rapidly transpiring plants, and cannot by itself account for the ascent of sap in tall trees.

The TRANSPIRATION PULL, explained by the COHESION-TENSION THEORY of Dixon and Joly, is now accepted as the main force. Its essentials are: (1) COHESION - water molecules attract one another strongly by hydrogen bonding and so cling together to form a continuous, unbroken column of water in the xylem; ADHESION - water molecules also stick to the walls of the narrow xylem vessels. Together these give the water column great tensile strength so that it does not break. (2) TRANSPIRATION PULL - as water evaporates from the moist walls of the mesophyll cells and diffuses out through the stomata (transpiration), the cells lose water and develop a lower (more negative) water potential; this pulls water from the xylem of the leaf, which in turn pulls the whole continuous water column upward from the roots, like a rope being pulled from the top. Thus transpiration acts as the 'engine' that lifts the sap, and the cohesion of water provides the unbroken 'rope'.

8.4 TRANSPIRATION - TYPES AND MECHANISM

TRANSPIRATION is the loss of water in the form of VAPOUR from the aerial parts (mainly leaves) of a plant. Only a very small fraction (about 1-2 per cent) of the water absorbed is used by the plant; the rest, over 95 per cent, is lost in transpiration. There are three TYPES:
 - STOMATAL transpiration: loss of water vapour through the STOMATA (tiny pores in the leaf epidermis). This accounts for the greatest part (about 80-90 per cent) of total transpiration.
 - CUTICULAR transpiration: loss of water directly through the CUTICLE (the waxy layer covering the epidermis). It is small and increases when the cuticle is thin, as in shade plants.
 - LENTICULAR transpiration: loss of water vapour through the LENTICELS - small pores in the bark of woody stems and in some fruits. It is the smallest of the three and continues even when stomata are closed.

MECHANISM OF STOMATAL OPENING AND CLOSING. Each stoma is bordered by two kidney-shaped (bean-shaped) GUARD CELLS whose inner wall (facing the pore) is THICK and inelastic while the outer wall is THIN and elastic. When the guard cells take up water and become TURGID, the thin outer walls stretch more than the thick inner walls, so the guard cells bulge outward and the pore OPENS. When the guard cells lose water and become FLACCID, they straighten and the pore CLOSES. What makes the guard cells gain water is a change in their solute (osmotic) concentration. The modern POTASSIUM-ION (K+) THEORY explains this: in light, guard cells actively pump in potassium ions (K+) from the neighbouring epidermal cells (accompanied by the opening of ion channels and the accumulation of malate). This raises the solute concentration inside the guard cells, LOWERS their water potential, so water enters by osmosis, the guard cells become turgid and the stoma OPENS. In darkness the K+ ions move out, water leaves the guard cells, they become flaccid and the stoma CLOSES. Thus stomata are generally open during the day (for photosynthesis) and closed at night.

8.5 FACTORS AFFECTING AND SIGNIFICANCE OF TRANSPIRATION

The rate of transpiration is controlled by ENVIRONMENTAL (external) and PLANT (internal) factors.
External factors: (a) LIGHT - opens the stomata and warms the leaf, increasing transpiration; (b) TEMPERATURE - higher temperature increases evaporation and the rate of transpiration; (c) HUMIDITY - high atmospheric humidity lowers the diffusion gradient and DECREASES transpiration, while dry air increases it; (d) WIND (air movement) - moderate wind removes the moist air around the leaf and speeds up transpiration; (e) available SOIL WATER - a good supply keeps transpiration high, while a shortage reduces it.
Internal (plant) factors: the number and distribution of stomata, the thickness of the cuticle, the leaf area, and features such as sunken stomata or hairs that reduce water loss in xerophytes.

SIGNIFICANCE (advantages) of transpiration: it creates the transpiration pull that drives the ascent of sap and the absorption of water; it helps in the upward transport and distribution of mineral salts; it COOLS the leaf surface by evaporative cooling and protects it from overheating in strong sun; and it helps maintain the turgidity of cells. DISADVANTAGES: transpiration is often described as a 'NECESSARY EVIL' because so much water is lost; excessive transpiration, especially when absorption cannot keep pace, leads to WILTING and, in dry conditions, may cause serious injury or death of the plant. Much of a plant's structure is a compromise between the need to take in carbon dioxide and the need to conserve water.

GUTTATION is the loss of water as LIQUID DROPLETS (not vapour) from the margins or tips of leaves through special pores called HYDATHODES. It occurs at night or in the early morning when the air is humid, transpiration is very low and ROOT PRESSURE is high, forcing water out through the hydathodes. The exuded liquid is not pure water; it contains dissolved salts and sugars. Guttation should not be confused with dew, which is atmospheric moisture that condenses on the leaf surface from outside.

8.6 TRANSLOCATION OF MINERALS AND ORGANIC SOLUTES

TRANSLOCATION is the transport of substances over long distances within the plant. Two separate streams operate: minerals and water move UPWARD in the XYLEM, while food (organic solutes) moves in the PHLOEM.

Transport of MINERAL IONS: minerals are absorbed from the soil mainly as IONS by the root cells. Their uptake is largely an ACTIVE process using ATP, allowing the plant to accumulate ions against a concentration gradient. Once in the xylem, the ions are carried UPWARD along with the transpiration stream to the growing regions, leaves and other parts. Minerals are also redistributed and are highly mobile - they can be withdrawn from older, senescing leaves and moved to young growing tissues through the phloem.

Translocation of ORGANIC SOLUTES (food): the sugars (mainly SUCROSE) made in the leaves by photosynthesis are transported through the PHLOEM (specifically the sieve tubes) to all parts of the plant that need food. This movement is described by the SOURCE-TO-SINK concept. A SOURCE is any part that makes or releases food (a photosynthesising mature leaf, or a storage organ that is exporting food); a SINK is any part that uses or stores food (roots, growing buds, flowers, fruits, seeds and tubers). Translocation in the phloem can occur in BOTH directions (up or down) depending on where the sources and sinks are, unlike the always-upward flow in the xylem.

The most widely accepted explanation is the MASS FLOW (PRESSURE FLOW) HYPOTHESIS proposed by Ernst Munch. According to it: at the SOURCE, sugar is actively loaded into the sieve tubes (phloem loading); this raises the solute concentration there, lowers the water potential, and water enters the sieve tubes from the neighbouring xylem by osmosis, building up a HIGH turgor pressure at the source end. At the SINK, sugar is unloaded and used or stored, so the solute concentration falls, water leaves the sieve tubes, and the turgor pressure there is LOW. The resulting pressure gradient (high at the source, low at the sink) drives a MASS FLOW of the sugary sap through the continuous sieve tubes from source to sink. Thus phloem transport is an energy-requiring (active at loading and unloading) process driven by an osmotically generated pressure gradient.

SUMMARY

- Diffusion is passive movement of molecules down a concentration gradient; imbibition is the swelling of hydrophilic solids (e.g. dry seeds) by absorbing water.
- Osmosis is the movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane from higher to lower water concentration; endosmosis (water in, cell turgid) and exosmosis (water out, cell shrinks).
- Osmotic pressure rises with solute concentration; turgor pressure (cell contents on wall) is balanced by wall pressure and keeps herbaceous parts firm.
- Water potential (psi) of pure water is zero; solutes make it negative. psi = solute potential (psi_s, negative) + pressure potential (psi_p). Water moves from higher to lower water potential.
- Plasmolysis is the shrinking of protoplasm from the wall in a hypertonic solution; deplasmolysis is recovery in water. It proves the membrane is selectively permeable and the cell is alive.
- Roots absorb water by osmosis through root hairs; water crosses via the apoplast (walls) and symplast (cytoplasm/plasmodesmata) pathways; the Casparian strip diverts water into the symplast at the endodermis. Passive absorption (transpiration-driven) vs active absorption (uses root energy, causes root pressure).
- Ascent of sap through the xylem is due mainly to the transpiration pull explained by the cohesion-tension theory (Dixon); root pressure plays only a minor role.
- Transpiration is loss of water vapour from aerial parts; types are stomatal (most), cuticular and lenticular. Stomata open when guard cells become turgid (K+ ions accumulate, water enters) and close when they become flaccid.
- Transpiration is affected by light, temperature, humidity, wind and soil water; it drives the ascent of sap and cools the leaf but causes large water loss ('necessary evil'). Guttation is loss of liquid water through hydathodes due to root pressure.
- Minerals are absorbed actively as ions and carried up in the xylem. Organic food (sucrose) is translocated in the phloem from source to sink by the mass flow (pressure flow) hypothesis of Munch.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Absorption, Transport and Water Loss in Plants (NIOS Senior Secondary Biology)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Answer briefly and precisely, using labelled sketches where helpful. Marks are shown against each question.

questions.question: Define osmosis. Distinguish between endosmosis and exosmosis.
questions.answer:
Osmosis is the movement of water (solvent) molecules from a region of higher water concentration (dilute solution) to a region of lower water concentration (concentrated solution) through a selectively permeable membrane.

Endosmosis is the movement of water INTO a cell when it is placed in a hypotonic (weaker) solution such as pure water; the cell swells and becomes turgid.

Exosmosis is the movement of water OUT of a cell when it is placed in a hypertonic (stronger) solution; the cell loses water and shrinks.
questions.explanation: Definition plus the in/out contrast.

questions.question: What is water potential? Name its two components and state the sign of each in a turgid cell.
questions.answer:
Water potential (psi) is the tendency of water to move from one region to another; the water potential of pure water is taken as zero, and adding solute makes it negative. Water moves from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) water potential.

Its two components are:
1. Solute potential (osmotic potential, psi_s) - always NEGATIVE because solutes lower water potential.
2. Pressure potential (psi_p) - POSITIVE in a turgid cell due to wall pressure.

They combine as psi = psi_s + psi_p.
questions.explanation: Definition, components and signs.

questions.question: What is plasmolysis? State two things it demonstrates about a plant cell.
questions.answer:
Plasmolysis is the shrinkage of the protoplasm (living contents) of a plant cell away from its cell wall when the cell is placed in a strongly hypertonic solution; water leaves the cell by exosmosis and the cell membrane pulls away from the wall.

It demonstrates that (1) the cell membrane is selectively (semi) permeable, and (2) the cell is alive - only a living cell with an intact membrane can be plasmolysed and later recover (deplasmolysis).
questions.explanation: Definition + membrane permeability + cell is living.

questions.question: Distinguish between the apoplast and symplast pathways of water movement in a root.
questions.answer:
Apoplast pathway: water moves through the non-living parts of the cells - the cell walls and intercellular spaces - without crossing any membrane. It is a fast route but is blocked at the endodermis by the Casparian strip.

Symplast pathway: water moves through the living cytoplasm of the cells, passing from one cell to the next through fine cytoplasmic bridges called plasmodesmata. It is comparatively slower.
questions.explanation: Non-living walls vs living cytoplasm; role of Casparian strip.

questions.question: Explain the cohesion-tension theory (transpiration pull) for the ascent of sap in tall trees.
questions.answer:
The ascent of sap is the upward movement of water and minerals from the roots to the leaves through the xylem. In tall trees the main force is the transpiration pull, explained by the cohesion-tension theory of Dixon and Joly.

1. Cohesion and adhesion: Water molecules attract one another strongly by hydrogen bonding (cohesion) and cling together to form a continuous, unbroken water column in the xylem. They also stick to the walls of the narrow xylem vessels (adhesion). Together these give the water column a high tensile strength, so it does not break even under tension.

2. Transpiration pull: As water evaporates from the moist walls of the mesophyll cells and diffuses out through the stomata (transpiration), these cells develop a lower (more negative) water potential. This pulls water from the leaf xylem, which in turn pulls the entire continuous column of water upward from the roots, rather like pulling a rope from the top.

Thus transpiration provides the 'pull' (the engine) and the cohesion of water provides the unbroken 'rope', together lifting the sap to the top of even the tallest trees. Root pressure plays only a minor role.
questions.explanation: Cohesion/adhesion give tensile strength; transpiration provides the pull.

questions.question: Name the three types of transpiration and state which contributes the most.
questions.answer:
The three types of transpiration are:
1. Stomatal transpiration - loss of water vapour through the stomata.
2. Cuticular transpiration - loss of water through the cuticle (waxy covering).
3. Lenticular transpiration - loss of water vapour through the lenticels of woody stems.

Stomatal transpiration contributes the most, about 80-90 per cent of the total.
questions.explanation: Three types; stomatal is greatest.

questions.question: Describe the mechanism of stomatal opening and closing, including the potassium-ion (K+) theory.
questions.answer:
Each stoma is bordered by two kidney-shaped guard cells whose inner wall (facing the pore) is thick and inelastic while the outer wall is thin and elastic.

When the guard cells absorb water and become TURGID, the thin outer walls stretch more than the thick inner walls, so the guard cells bulge outward (curve away from each other) and the pore OPENS. When the guard cells lose water and become FLACCID, they straighten and the pore CLOSES.

The change in turgidity is caused by a change in the solute concentration of the guard cells, explained by the potassium-ion (K+) theory: In light, the guard cells actively pump in potassium ions (K+) from the neighbouring epidermal cells (with accumulation of malate). This raises the solute concentration, LOWERS the water potential of the guard cells, so water enters by osmosis, the guard cells become turgid and the stoma opens.

In darkness, the K+ ions move out, water leaves the guard cells, they become flaccid and the stoma closes. Hence stomata are usually open in the day (for photosynthesis) and closed at night.
questions.explanation: Guard-cell wall thickening + K+ theory of turgor change.

questions.question: List any four factors that affect the rate of transpiration and state how each acts.
questions.answer:
1. Light: opens the stomata and warms the leaf, so it increases transpiration.
2. Temperature: a higher temperature increases evaporation and raises the rate of transpiration.
3. Humidity: high atmospheric humidity lowers the diffusion gradient and decreases transpiration; dry air increases it.
4. Wind (air movement): moderate wind removes moist air around the leaf and speeds up transpiration.
(Availability of soil water is another factor: ample water keeps transpiration high.)
questions.explanation: Light, temperature, humidity, wind with direction of effect.

questions.question: Why is transpiration called a 'necessary evil'? Give one advantage and one disadvantage.
questions.answer:
Transpiration is called a 'necessary evil' because, although a great deal of water is lost from the plant (over 95 per cent of what is absorbed), the process cannot be entirely avoided and it also brings important benefits.

Advantage: it creates the transpiration pull that drives the ascent of sap and the absorption of water and minerals, and it cools the leaf by evaporative cooling.

Disadvantage: excessive water loss, especially when absorption cannot keep pace, causes wilting and may injure or kill the plant in dry conditions.
questions.explanation: Necessary (benefits/unavoidable) yet evil (large water loss).

questions.question: Explain the mass flow (pressure flow) hypothesis of Munch for the translocation of organic food in the phloem.
questions.answer:
Sugars (mainly sucrose) made in the leaves are translocated through the phloem (sieve tubes) from a SOURCE (a food-making or food-releasing part, such as a mature leaf) to a SINK (a food-using or food-storing part, such as roots, fruits or growing buds). Ernst Munch's mass flow (pressure flow) hypothesis explains this:

At the SOURCE: sugar is actively loaded into the sieve tubes (phloem loading). This raises the solute concentration, lowers the water potential, and water enters the sieve tubes from the neighbouring xylem by osmosis, building up a HIGH turgor pressure at the source end.

At the SINK: sugar is unloaded and used or stored, so the solute concentration falls, water leaves the sieve tubes, and the turgor pressure there becomes LOW.

The difference in turgor pressure (high at the source, low at the sink) drives a mass flow of the sugary sap through the continuous sieve tubes from source to sink. Because loading and unloading require energy, phloem transport is an active, energy-requiring process. Unlike the always-upward xylem flow, phloem flow can be in either direction depending on the positions of sources and sinks.
questions.explanation: Source loading (high P) to sink unloading (low P) drives bulk flow.

questions.question: Define diffusion and give one example in plants.
questions.answer: Diffusion is the net movement of molecules or ions from a region of their higher concentration to a region of their lower concentration, down a concentration gradient, without using metabolic energy. Example: the entry of carbon dioxide and exit of oxygen and water vapour through the stomata.
questions.explanation: Definition + gaseous exchange example.

questions.question: Distinguish between osmotic pressure, turgor pressure and wall pressure.
questions.answer: Osmotic pressure is the pressure that must be applied to a solution to just prevent the entry of water into it through a semipermeable membrane; it increases with solute concentration. Turgor pressure is the pressure exerted by the swollen cell contents against the cell wall when water enters the cell. Wall pressure is the equal and opposite pressure exerted by the rigid cell wall against the protoplast.
questions.explanation: Three related pressures distinguished.

questions.question: What is imbibition? Mention one importance of it.
questions.answer: Imbibition is a special type of diffusion in which water is absorbed by solid hydrophilic colloidal substances (such as the cellulose, starch and proteins of dry seeds), causing them to swell. Its importance: the imbibition pressure developed helps a germinating seed to swell and the seedling to push through the soil (it can even split rocks).
questions.explanation: Definition + role in germination.

questions.question: A raisin swells when kept in water but shrivels in strong sugar syrup. Explain both observations.
questions.answer: In water (a hypotonic medium) the water potential outside is higher than inside the raisin, so water enters the raisin cells by endosmosis and it swells and becomes turgid. In strong sugar syrup (a hypertonic medium) the water potential outside is lower than inside, so water leaves the cells by exosmosis and the raisin loses water and shrivels.
questions.explanation: Endosmosis vs exosmosis explained by water potential.

questions.question: Define water potential. Why is the water potential of a solution negative?
questions.answer: Water potential (psi) is the tendency of water to move from one region to another; water flows from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) water potential. The water potential of pure water is taken as zero. When solute is added, it lowers the free energy of water, so the water potential of a solution becomes negative (less than zero). The more concentrated the solution, the more negative its water potential.
questions.explanation: Definition + effect of solutes.

questions.question: Explain plasmolysis and deplasmolysis with reference to the type of solution used.
questions.answer: Plasmolysis is the shrinkage of the protoplasm away from the cell wall when a cell is placed in a hypertonic (strong) solution; water leaves the cell by exosmosis and the membrane pulls away from the wall, and turgor pressure falls to zero. Deplasmolysis is the recovery that follows when the plasmolysed cell is placed back in a hypotonic solution or pure water; water re-enters by endosmosis and the protoplast swells to press against the wall again.
questions.explanation: Hypertonic causes plasmolysis; pure water reverses it.

questions.question: Salting of soil can kill crop plants. Explain in terms of water relations.
questions.answer: Adding excess salt (or too much fertiliser) to the soil makes the soil solution hypertonic - its water potential becomes lower (more negative) than that of the root cell sap. Water therefore moves OUT of the root cells by exosmosis instead of into them, the cells become plasmolysed and cannot absorb water. Deprived of water, the root cells are damaged and the plant wilts and may die. This is why over-salting or over-fertilising harms crops.
questions.explanation: Hypertonic soil causes exosmosis/plasmolysis of roots.

questions.question: State two functions of root hairs.
questions.answer: 1. They greatly increase the surface area of the root for the absorption of water and mineral salts. 2. They are in close contact with the film of water around soil particles and absorb water by osmosis (and ions by active uptake).
questions.explanation: Surface area + absorption of water/ions.

questions.question: Describe the pathway of water from the soil to the xylem of a root.
questions.answer: Water in the soil is absorbed by the root hairs by osmosis, because the cell sap has a lower (more negative) water potential than the dilute soil solution. From cell to cell across the cortex the water travels by two pathways - the apoplast (through the cell walls and intercellular spaces) and the symplast (through the cytoplasm via plasmodesmata). At the endodermis the Casparian strip blocks the apoplast and forces the water into the symplast, from where it passes on into the xylem to be carried upward.
questions.explanation: Root hair osmosis, apoplast/symplast, Casparian strip, xylem.

questions.question: Distinguish between active and passive absorption of water.
questions.answer: Passive absorption occurs during rapid transpiration: the pull created by transpiration in the leaves is transmitted down to the roots, which act merely as passive surfaces through which water is drawn in; no metabolic energy of the root is used. Active absorption is slow and uses the metabolic energy (respiration/ATP) of the root cells to take in water, is linked with active ion uptake, causes root pressure, and is significant when transpiration is low (e.g. at night).
questions.explanation: Passive = transpiration-driven, no root energy; active = uses ATP.

questions.question: What is root pressure? How is it demonstrated?
questions.answer: Root pressure is a positive hydrostatic pressure that develops in the xylem of the roots as a result of the active absorption of water and ions by living root cells. It is demonstrated by guttation (exudation of water droplets at leaf margins) and by the bleeding of sap from a freshly cut stem stump.
questions.explanation: Definition + guttation/bleeding evidence.

questions.question: State the role of cohesion and adhesion in the ascent of sap.
questions.answer: Cohesion is the mutual attraction between water molecules due to hydrogen bonding; it makes the water in the xylem form a continuous, unbroken column with high tensile strength, so it does not snap when pulled. Adhesion is the attraction of water molecules to the walls of the narrow xylem vessels, which helps hold the water column in place. Together they allow the transpiration pull to draw the whole column upward without breaking.
questions.explanation: Cohesion holds column together; adhesion sticks it to walls.

questions.question: Why is root pressure not sufficient to explain the ascent of sap in tall trees?
questions.answer: Root pressure is small (rarely more than 1-2 atmospheres) and can raise water only a short distance up the stem. It is absent in many tall trees and in plants that are transpiring rapidly, and it disappears in dry conditions. Therefore it cannot lift water to the tops of tall trees, which may be over a hundred metres high; the transpiration pull is needed for that.
questions.explanation: Root pressure is small and often absent, so insufficient.

questions.question: Name and define the three types of transpiration.
questions.answer: 1. Stomatal transpiration - loss of water vapour through the stomata (the greatest part). 2. Cuticular transpiration - loss of water through the cuticle (waxy covering of the epidermis). 3. Lenticular transpiration - loss of water vapour through the lenticels of woody stems and some fruits (the smallest part).
questions.explanation: Three types with sites.

questions.question: Describe the structure of guard cells that helps in the opening and closing of a stoma.
questions.answer: Each stoma is bordered by two kidney-shaped (bean-shaped) guard cells. The inner wall of each guard cell, facing the pore, is thick and inelastic, while the outer wall is thin and elastic. Because of this unequal thickening, when the guard cells become turgid the thin outer walls stretch more and the cells curve outward, opening the pore; when they become flaccid they straighten and the pore closes. Guard cells also contain chloroplasts, unlike other epidermal cells.
questions.explanation: Unequal wall thickening + turgidity controls the pore.

questions.question: Explain, using the K+ theory, why stomata usually open in the day and close at night.
questions.answer: In light (day), the guard cells actively take up potassium ions (K+) from the neighbouring epidermal cells. This raises the solute concentration and lowers the water potential of the guard cells, so water enters them by osmosis, they become turgid and the stoma opens - allowing carbon dioxide in for photosynthesis. At night, in the dark, K+ ions move out of the guard cells; their water potential rises, water leaves, the guard cells become flaccid and the stoma closes.
questions.explanation: K+ influx in light opens; K+ efflux in dark closes.

questions.question: Relate the change in water potential of guard cells to stomatal movement.
questions.answer: When solutes such as K+ ions (and malate) accumulate in the guard cells, their water potential becomes lower (more negative) than that of the surrounding cells. Water therefore moves into the guard cells by osmosis, they become turgid, and the stoma opens. When the solutes are lost, the water potential of the guard cells rises, water moves out, they become flaccid, and the stoma closes. Thus stomatal movement is governed by osmotically driven changes in the guard cells' water potential and turgor.
questions.explanation: Lower psi draws water in (open); higher psi lets water out (close).

questions.question: List the external factors affecting transpiration and state the effect of each.
questions.answer: Light - opens stomata and warms the leaf, increasing transpiration. Temperature - a rise increases evaporation and the rate of transpiration. Humidity - high humidity decreases transpiration (small diffusion gradient); dry air increases it. Wind - moderate wind removes moist air around the leaf and speeds up transpiration. Availability of soil water - ample water keeps transpiration high, while a shortage reduces it.
questions.explanation: Light, temperature, humidity, wind, soil water and their effects.

questions.question: State three advantages (significance) of transpiration.
questions.answer: 1. It creates the transpiration pull, which drives the ascent of sap and the absorption of water. 2. It helps in the upward transport and distribution of mineral salts in the plant. 3. It cools the leaf surface by evaporative cooling, protecting it from overheating in strong sunlight (it also helps maintain cell turgidity).
questions.explanation: Three benefits of transpiration.

questions.question: Distinguish between transpiration and guttation.
questions.answer: Transpiration is the loss of water in the form of vapour, mainly through the stomata of the leaves, occurring largely during the day; the water lost is pure. Guttation is the loss of water in the form of liquid droplets through special pores called hydathodes at the margins or tips of leaves, occurring at night or early morning when transpiration is low and root pressure is high; the exuded liquid contains dissolved salts and sugars.
questions.explanation: Vapour/stomata/day vs liquid/hydathodes/night.

questions.question: Explain the source-to-sink concept of translocation with examples.
questions.answer: In phloem transport, a SOURCE is any part of the plant that makes or releases food - for example a mature, photosynthesising leaf, or a storage organ that is exporting food. A SINK is any part that uses or stores food - for example roots, growing buds, flowers, fruits, seeds and tubers. Food (mainly sucrose) is translocated from source to sink. Because sources and sinks may lie in different directions, phloem transport can occur both upward and downward, unlike the always-upward xylem flow.
questions.explanation: Source makes food, sink uses/stores; bidirectional.

questions.question: How are mineral ions absorbed and transported in a plant?
questions.answer: Mineral salts are absorbed from the soil mainly as ions by the root cells. Their uptake is largely an active process using metabolic energy (ATP), which allows the plant to accumulate ions even against a concentration gradient. Once in the root xylem, the ions are carried upward along with the transpiration stream (the ascent of sap) to the stem, leaves and growing regions. Minerals are also mobile and can be redistributed through the phloem, being withdrawn from old leaves and sent to young tissues.
questions.explanation: Active uptake as ions; upward transport in xylem with transpiration stream.

questions.question: Describe an experiment or observations to explain osmosis, endosmosis and exosmosis in plant cells.
questions.answer:
Osmosis is the movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane from a region of higher water concentration (dilute solution) to one of lower water concentration (concentrated solution).

Endosmosis: If pieces of potato or a plant cell are placed in pure water or a very dilute (hypotonic) solution, the water potential outside is higher than that of the cell sap. Water therefore moves INTO the cells by osmosis; the cells swell, become turgid and firm. This inward movement is endosmosis.

Exosmosis: If the same cells are placed in a strong (hypertonic) salt or sugar solution, the water potential outside is lower than that of the cell sap. Water moves OUT of the cells by osmosis; the cells lose water, shrink and become flaccid, and their protoplasm may pull away from the wall (plasmolysis). This outward movement is exosmosis.

The direction of movement is decided by the water potential (or concentration) gradient: water always moves from higher to lower water potential through the selectively permeable membrane. A classic demonstration uses a thistle-funnel osmometer, in which a concentrated sugar solution enclosed by a membrane draws in water and its level rises, showing osmosis and the development of osmotic pressure.
questions.explanation: Define osmosis; endosmosis in hypotonic, exosmosis in hypertonic; osmometer demo.

questions.question: Explain water potential and its components, and use them to predict the direction of water movement between two cells.
questions.answer:
Water potential (psi) is the tendency of water to move from one region to another; it is measured relative to pure water, whose water potential is taken as zero. Adding solute or applying tension lowers water potential (makes it negative), while positive pressure raises it. Water always moves from a region of higher (less negative) water potential to one of lower (more negative) water potential.

Components: psi = psi_s + psi_p.
- Solute potential (osmotic potential, psi_s) is the lowering of water potential due to dissolved solutes; it is always negative and becomes more negative as the solution gets more concentrated.
- Pressure potential (psi_p) is the effect of pressure; in a turgid cell the wall pressure makes psi_p positive.

Predicting water movement between two cells: Suppose cell A has psi = -0.8 units and cell B has psi = -0.5 units. Because water moves from higher to lower water potential, and -0.5 is higher (less negative) than -0.8, water will move FROM cell B (psi = -0.5) TO cell A (psi = -0.8) until their water potentials become equal. In general, the cell with the higher (less negative) water potential loses water to the cell with the lower (more negative) water potential. This is exactly how water passes from cell to cell across the root and up the plant.
questions.explanation: psi = psi_s + psi_p; water flows to lower psi; worked cell comparison.

questions.question: Describe how water is absorbed by roots and moves across the root to the xylem, mentioning the apoplast and symplast pathways and the Casparian strip.
questions.answer:
Water and dissolved minerals are absorbed mainly through the root hairs, which are fine, thin-walled outgrowths of the epidermal cells near the root tips. Root hairs greatly increase the surface area for absorption and lie in close contact with the film of water around soil particles.

The cell sap of a root hair is more concentrated (has a lower, more negative water potential) than the dilute soil solution, so water enters the root hair by osmosis. From there it passes across the cortex towards the xylem by two pathways:
1. Apoplast pathway - water moves through the non-living cell walls and intercellular spaces without crossing any membrane; this is a fast route.
2. Symplast pathway - water moves through the living cytoplasm of the cells, passing from cell to cell through fine cytoplasmic connections called plasmodesmata.

At the endodermis, a band of waterproof suberin called the Casparian strip is present in the radial and transverse walls. This strip blocks the apoplast pathway and forces all the water to pass through the living cells (the symplast). This lets the endodermis control what enters the xylem. Beyond the endodermis the water enters the xylem vessels and is carried upward as the ascent of sap.

Absorption may be passive (drawn in by transpiration pull, using no root energy) or active (using the root's metabolic energy, causing root pressure).
questions.explanation: Root-hair osmosis; apoplast/symplast; Casparian strip diverts to symplast; xylem.

questions.question: Describe the ascent of sap, comparing the roles of root pressure and transpiration pull.
questions.answer:
The ascent of sap is the upward movement of water and dissolved minerals from the roots to the leaves through the xylem. The xylem vessels and tracheids form continuous, non-living tubes ideal for this bulk flow. Two mechanisms are involved.

Root pressure: This is a positive hydrostatic pressure that develops in the root xylem due to the active absorption of water and ions by living root cells. It can push water a little way up the stem and is shown by guttation and by the bleeding of a cut stump. However, root pressure is small (usually 1-2 atmospheres), is absent in many tall trees and in rapidly transpiring plants, and so cannot by itself raise water to the top of a tall tree. It therefore plays only a minor role.

Transpiration pull (cohesion-tension theory of Dixon and Joly): This is the main force. As water evaporates from the mesophyll cell walls and diffuses out through the stomata (transpiration), these cells develop a lower water potential and pull water from the leaf xylem. Because water molecules cohere strongly by hydrogen bonding (cohesion) and stick to the xylem walls (adhesion), the water in the xylem forms a continuous column with great tensile strength. The pull at the top is thus transmitted right down the unbroken column to the roots, drawing water up like a rope pulled from above.

Comparison: root pressure is a 'push' from below, small and often absent; transpiration pull is a 'pull' from above, large and continuous, and is responsible for the ascent of sap in tall trees.
questions.explanation: Root pressure (minor push) vs transpiration pull (main pull, cohesion-tension).

questions.question: Define transpiration, describe its types, and explain the structure of a stoma.
questions.answer:
Transpiration is the loss of water in the form of vapour from the aerial parts (mainly the leaves) of a plant. Only about 1-2 per cent of the water absorbed is used by the plant; over 95 per cent is lost in transpiration.

Types:
1. Stomatal transpiration - loss of water vapour through the stomata; it accounts for the greatest part (about 80-90 per cent) of the total.
2. Cuticular transpiration - loss of water directly through the cuticle (the waxy layer over the epidermis); it is small and greater when the cuticle is thin.
3. Lenticular transpiration - loss of water vapour through the lenticels (pores in the bark of woody stems); it is the smallest and continues even when the stomata are closed.

Structure of a stoma: A stoma is a tiny pore in the leaf epidermis bordered by two kidney-shaped guard cells. The inner wall of each guard cell (facing the pore) is thick and inelastic, while the outer wall is thin and elastic. Guard cells contain chloroplasts. Around them are subsidiary (accessory) cells. When the guard cells become turgid the pore opens; when they become flaccid it closes. Stomata are usually more numerous on the lower surface of a leaf, which reduces water loss.
questions.explanation: Definition; stomatal/cuticular/lenticular; guard-cell structure of a stoma.

questions.question: Explain in detail the mechanism of opening and closing of stomata according to the potassium-ion theory.
questions.answer:
Stomatal movements depend on changes in the turgidity of the two guard cells that border each stoma. The inner wall of a guard cell (next to the pore) is thick and inelastic, while the outer wall is thin and elastic. When the guard cells gain water and become turgid, the thin outer walls stretch more than the thick inner walls, so the guard cells curve outward (away from each other) and the pore OPENS. When they lose water and become flaccid, they straighten and the pore CLOSES.

What makes the guard cells gain or lose water is a change in their solute concentration, explained by the potassium-ion (K+) theory:
- Opening (in light): the guard cells actively pump in potassium ions (K+) from the neighbouring epidermal cells; ion channels open and the organic acid malate accumulates. This raises the solute concentration inside the guard cells and LOWERS their water potential (makes it more negative). Water therefore enters the guard cells from the surrounding cells by osmosis, the guard cells become turgid, and the stoma opens.
- Closing (in darkness): the K+ ions move back out of the guard cells; the solute concentration falls, the water potential rises, water leaves the guard cells by osmosis, they become flaccid, and the stoma closes.

Because light triggers K+ uptake, stomata are generally open during the day (permitting carbon dioxide entry for photosynthesis) and closed at night (reducing water loss). Factors such as carbon dioxide concentration and the hormone abscisic acid (which closes stomata under water stress) also influence the movement.
questions.explanation: Wall thickening + K+ influx lowers psi (open), K+ efflux raises psi (close).

questions.question: Discuss the factors affecting transpiration and evaluate why transpiration is called a 'necessary evil'.
questions.answer:
Factors affecting transpiration:
External (environmental) factors - (a) Light opens the stomata and warms the leaf, increasing transpiration. (b) A rise in temperature increases evaporation and the rate of transpiration. (c) High atmospheric humidity lowers the diffusion gradient and decreases transpiration, while dry air increases it. (d) Moderate wind removes the moist air around the leaf and speeds up transpiration. (e) A good supply of soil water keeps transpiration high, while a shortage reduces it.
Internal (plant) factors - the number and distribution of stomata, the thickness of the cuticle, the total leaf area, and adaptations such as sunken stomata or hairs in xerophytes that reduce water loss.

'Necessary evil': Transpiration is called a necessary evil because it has both essential benefits and serious drawbacks. Benefits (why it is 'necessary'): it creates the transpiration pull that drives the ascent of sap and the absorption of water; it helps distribute mineral salts through the plant; and it cools the leaf by evaporative cooling, protecting it from overheating. Drawbacks (why it is an 'evil'): a plant loses enormous amounts of water (over 95 per cent of what it absorbs); when absorption cannot keep pace with this loss the plant wilts, and in dry conditions excessive transpiration can injure or kill it. Because the same stomatal openings that let carbon dioxide in for photosynthesis inevitably let water vapour out, transpiration cannot be avoided - so the plant must tolerate the loss while gaining its benefits, which is why it is described as a necessary evil.
questions.explanation: Factors (external + internal); benefits vs heavy water loss = necessary evil.

questions.question: Explain the translocation of organic solutes in the phloem, including the source-sink concept and the mass flow hypothesis of Munch.
questions.answer:
Translocation of organic solutes is the transport of food, mainly the sugar sucrose made in the leaves by photosynthesis, through the phloem (sieve tubes) to all parts of the plant.

Source-sink concept: A SOURCE is any part that makes or releases food - a mature, photosynthesising leaf, or a storage organ that is exporting food. A SINK is any part that uses or stores food - roots, growing buds, flowers, fruits, seeds and tubers. Food moves from source to sink. Because sources and sinks may lie in different directions, phloem transport can go either upward or downward, unlike the always-upward flow in the xylem.

Mass flow (pressure flow) hypothesis of Munch: According to Ernst Munch,
- At the source, sugar is actively loaded into the sieve tubes (phloem loading). This raises the solute concentration, lowers the water potential, and water enters the sieve tubes from the neighbouring xylem by osmosis, building up a HIGH turgor pressure at the source end.
- At the sink, sugar is unloaded and used or stored, so the solute concentration falls, water leaves the sieve tubes, and the turgor pressure there becomes LOW.
- The resulting pressure gradient (high at the source, low at the sink) drives a mass flow of the sugary sap through the continuous sieve tubes from source to sink.

Because loading and unloading of sugar require energy, phloem transport is an active, energy-requiring process driven by an osmotically generated pressure gradient. This hypothesis explains the observed bulk flow of food in plants.
questions.explanation: Source/sink; Munch: loading (high P) to unloading (low P) drives mass flow.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A student places three identical strips of potato tissue into three beakers: beaker A contains pure water, beaker B a very strong salt solution, and beaker C a solution isotonic with the cell sap. After an hour the strips are examined.
(a) In which beaker will the strip become firm and turgid, and why?
(b) In which beaker will the strip become soft and flaccid, and why?
(c) What happens to the strip in beaker C?
(d) Name the process responsible for these changes.
questions.answer:
(a) In beaker A (pure water). The water potential outside is higher than inside the cells, so water enters by endosmosis, the cells become turgid and the strip becomes firm.
(b) In beaker B (strong salt solution). The water potential outside is lower than inside, so water leaves the cells by exosmosis, the cells become flaccid and the strip becomes soft.
(c) In beaker C (isotonic solution) there is no net movement of water, so the strip remains unchanged in firmness.
(d) Osmosis (endosmosis in A, exosmosis in B).
questions.explanation: Hypotonic->turgid, hypertonic->flaccid, isotonic->no change; osmosis.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Water potential (psi) describes the water status of a cell and is the sum of solute potential (psi_s) and pressure potential (psi_p). Pure water has psi = 0. Cell X has psi = -0.9 MPa and cell Y has psi = -0.4 MPa, and they are in contact.
(a) Write the equation relating psi to its components.
(b) What is the sign of the solute potential of a cell, and why?
(c) Between cells X and Y, in which direction will water move?
(d) What is the water potential of pure water?
questions.answer:
(a) psi = psi_s + psi_p (water potential = solute potential + pressure potential).
(b) The solute potential is negative, because dissolved solutes lower the water potential below that of pure water.
(c) Water moves from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) water potential, i.e. from cell Y (psi = -0.4 MPa) to cell X (psi = -0.9 MPa).
(d) The water potential of pure water is zero.
questions.explanation: psi=psi_s+psi_p; psi_s negative; water Y->X; pure water psi=0.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
When onion-peel cells are mounted in a strong sugar solution and observed under a microscope, the protoplasm is seen to shrink away from the cell walls. On replacing the sugar solution with water, the protoplasm expands back to the wall.
(a) Name the two processes observed.
(b) What kind of solution causes the first process?
(c) State two conclusions this experiment allows about the cell.
(d) Would the same result be seen with dead cells?
questions.answer:
(a) The shrinking of the protoplasm is plasmolysis; the expansion back on adding water is deplasmolysis.
(b) A hypertonic (strong sugar) solution causes plasmolysis (water leaves by exosmosis).
(c) It shows that (i) the cell membrane is selectively (semi) permeable and (ii) the cell is alive, since only a living cell can be plasmolysed and recover.
(d) No. Dead cells cannot be plasmolysed because their membranes are no longer selectively permeable.
questions.explanation: Plasmolysis/deplasmolysis; hypertonic; membrane selective + cell alive; not in dead cells.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Water absorbed by root hairs crosses the cortex to reach the xylem by two routes. At the endodermis a band of suberin controls the flow.
(a) Name the two pathways of water movement across the root.
(b) Through which structures does water pass in the symplast pathway?
(c) Name the suberised band at the endodermis and state its function.
(d) Why does the cell sap of a root hair draw water in from the soil?
questions.answer:
(a) The apoplast pathway (through cell walls and intercellular spaces) and the symplast pathway (through the living cytoplasm).
(b) In the symplast pathway water passes from cell to cell through the cytoplasm via fine bridges called plasmodesmata.
(c) The Casparian strip; it blocks the apoplast pathway so that water is forced into the symplast, letting the endodermis control what enters the xylem.
(d) The cell sap of the root hair has a lower (more negative) water potential than the dilute soil solution, so water moves in by osmosis.
questions.explanation: Apoplast/symplast; plasmodesmata; Casparian strip diverts to symplast; osmosis into root hair.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
In a tall tree, water rises through the xylem to leaves more than 50 m above the ground. Root pressure is measured to be only about 1-2 atmospheres.
(a) Name the process by which water rises in the xylem.
(b) Why can root pressure not account for this rise?
(c) Name the theory that explains the main force and the scientists associated with it.
(d) State the two properties of water that keep the water column unbroken.
questions.answer:
(a) The ascent of sap (upward movement of water and minerals through the xylem).
(b) Root pressure is too small (only 1-2 atmospheres), is absent in many tall trees and in rapidly transpiring plants, so it cannot lift water more than 50 m.
(c) The cohesion-tension theory (transpiration pull), associated with Dixon and Joly.
(d) Cohesion (hydrogen bonding between water molecules) and adhesion (attraction of water to the xylem walls), which together give the column high tensile strength.
questions.explanation: Ascent of sap; root pressure too small; cohesion-tension (Dixon & Joly); cohesion + adhesion.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A plant loses water vapour from its leaves and stems by different routes. Most is lost through pores in the leaf epidermis, some through the waxy covering, and a little through pores in the bark.
(a) Name the three types of transpiration described.
(b) Which type accounts for the greatest water loss?
(c) Name the structures involved in each type.
(d) About what percentage of absorbed water is lost by transpiration?
questions.answer:
(a) Stomatal, cuticular and lenticular transpiration.
(b) Stomatal transpiration accounts for the greatest water loss (about 80-90 per cent).
(c) Stomatal - through the stomata; cuticular - through the cuticle (waxy layer); lenticular - through the lenticels of woody stems.
(d) Over 95 per cent of the water absorbed is lost by transpiration (only about 1-2 per cent is used by the plant).
questions.explanation: Three types; stomatal greatest; stomata/cuticle/lenticels; >95 per cent lost.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Stomatal opening depends on the turgidity of the guard cells. In light, potassium ions accumulate in the guard cells; in darkness they leave.
(a) What happens to the water potential of guard cells when K+ ions accumulate?
(b) How does this cause the stoma to open?
(c) Why do the guard cells bulge outward on becoming turgid?
(d) When do stomata of most plants close, and why?
questions.answer:
(a) When K+ ions (and malate) accumulate, the solute concentration rises and the water potential of the guard cells falls (becomes more negative).
(b) Because their water potential is now lower than that of the surrounding cells, water enters the guard cells by osmosis; they become turgid, curve outward and the pore opens.
(c) The inner wall (facing the pore) is thick and inelastic while the outer wall is thin and elastic, so on becoming turgid the thin outer walls stretch more and the cells bulge outward.
(d) Stomata of most plants close at night (in darkness), because K+ ions leave the guard cells, water moves out, they become flaccid and the pore closes.
questions.explanation: K+ lowers psi; osmosis makes guard cells turgid -> open; unequal walls bulge; close in dark.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A gardener notices that potted plants wilt more on a hot, dry, windy afternoon than on a cool, humid, still morning. On some humid mornings, tiny water droplets appear at the tips of the leaves.
(a) Explain why transpiration is greater on the hot, dry, windy afternoon.
(b) Why does high humidity in the morning reduce transpiration?
(c) Name the process that produces the water droplets at the leaf tips and the pores involved.
(d) State one advantage and one disadvantage of transpiration.
questions.answer:
(a) High temperature increases evaporation, dry air provides a steep diffusion gradient, and wind removes the moist air around the leaves - all three increase the rate of transpiration, so the plant loses water faster and wilts.
(b) High humidity means the air already holds much water vapour, so the diffusion gradient between the leaf and the air is small; less water vapour diffuses out and transpiration is reduced.
(c) Guttation, which occurs through special pores called hydathodes (caused by root pressure when transpiration is low).
(d) Advantage: it drives the ascent of sap and cools the leaf. Disadvantage: it causes large water loss that can lead to wilting or injury.
questions.explanation: Heat/dry/wind raise transpiration; humidity lowers gradient; guttation via hydathodes; benefit vs water loss.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Sugar made in the leaves is transported through the phloem to other parts of the plant. Ernst Munch explained this by a pressure gradient set up by osmosis.
(a) Name the process and the tissue involved.
(b) Define source and sink with one example of each.
(c) According to the mass flow hypothesis, where is the turgor pressure highest and lowest?
(d) In which direction can phloem transport occur, compared with xylem transport?
questions.answer:
(a) Translocation of organic food, which takes place through the phloem (sieve tubes).
(b) A source is a part that makes or releases food, e.g. a mature photosynthesising leaf; a sink is a part that uses or stores food, e.g. a root, fruit or growing bud.
(c) According to the mass flow (pressure flow) hypothesis, turgor pressure is highest at the source (where sugar is loaded and water enters) and lowest at the sink (where sugar is unloaded and water leaves).
(d) Phloem transport can occur in both directions (upward or downward) depending on the positions of sources and sinks, whereas xylem transport is always upward.
questions.explanation: Translocation in phloem; source/sink; pressure high at source, low at sink; bidirectional.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Dry gram (chickpea) seeds are placed in water and, after some hours, are found to have swollen greatly. When such swelling seeds are packed tightly in a closed steel container filled with water, the container may bulge or burst.
(a) Name the process by which the dry seeds swell.
(b) Why are the seeds able to take up water in this way?
(c) What is the force developed during this process called, and what does the bursting of the container show?
(d) State one biological importance of this process.
questions.answer:
(a) Imbibition (a special type of diffusion in which hydrophilic solids absorb water and swell).
(b) The seeds contain hydrophilic (water-loving) colloids such as cellulose, starch and proteins, which strongly attract and absorb water, causing the seeds to swell.
(c) The force is called imbibition pressure; the bursting of the container shows that a very great pressure is developed during imbibition.
(d) It helps a germinating seed to swell and the seedling to break through the seed coat and push out of the soil (imbibition can even split rocks).
questions.explanation: Imbibition; hydrophilic colloids; imbibition pressure (great force); aids germination.
